clue.text: Live in a dream, initially sleeping?

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted
one thing being in another means it sits inside it, wrapped by the outer letters

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter of dream
to be is to live or exist

explanation.surface: Someone drifting through life in a dreamlike haze, half asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' looks like the definition but supplies BE, which goes inside A plus the first letter of dream to make ABED.
explanation.definitionFit: Abed is an old-fashioned word meaning lying in one's bed, typically asleep or resting there.

clue.text: Country boy at day’s end: traditional scourge of 13ac/26ac guests?

indicators.note: an end is the final point, so the last letter alone is kept

blocks.note: a country is a land
a lad is a boy
last letter of day

explanation.surface: A country boy finishing his day, and the stern figure who rules over guests at a seaside guesthouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 13ac/26ac means SEASIDE B AND B: a B and B is a British bed-and-breakfast guesthouse, whose proprietor is famously strict with guests.
explanation.definitionFit: The woman running a seaside boarding house is a stock comic figure, notorious for rules about curfews and wet towels.

clue.text: Ball caught by female trainer?

indicators.note: something caught is held in the catcher's grasp, so it ends up enclosed

blocks.note: she is the female pronoun
O is round like a ball

explanation.surface: A woman coach catching a ball during practice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trainer' suggests a coach, but here it is a sports shoe, as British English calls a sneaker a trainer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a trainer is a sneaker or running shoe, so it is a kind of footwear.

clue.text: Treat unnamed Crimean wounded outside the church

indicators.note: without a name means losing the abbreviation for name, a single letter
something wounded is damaged and knocked out of shape, so its letters are rearranged
being outside something means surrounding it on both sides

blocks.note: the word minus N, the abbreviation for name
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Caring for an anonymous soldier wounded in the Crimean War, outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unnamed' is the trick: N stands for name, so dropping it leaves six letters to rearrange before they wrap the church abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice cream is a classic sweet indulgence, the sort of thing you would buy someone as a reward.

clue.text: Politician on way back – threat to the cabinet?

indicators.note: in a down clue one thing on another sits above it, so the first piece is written before the second
going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters are read in reverse

blocks.note: a Tory is a British Conservative politician
Rd is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A politician on the comeback trail who poses a danger to the government cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet' suggests government ministers, but it is a wooden cupboard; the whole of politician-plus-road is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Dry rot is a fungus that decays timber, so it endangers wooden furniture such as a cupboard.

clue.text: Short-lived construction scandal set to blow up

indicators.note: an explosion scatters things, so the letters land in a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A building-industry scandal that is about to explode in the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Construction' and 'scandal' suggest a building-trade story; the definition is cryptic, as the tide soon washes the structure away.
explanation.definitionFit: A model castle built from beach sand lasts only until the tide comes in, so it is temporary.

clue.text: It contains rain a lot

blocks.note: first meaning: a pail, a container
second meaning: a British verb for pouring with rain

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence about something holding rainwater, but splits after 'contains'; to bucket down is British slang for heavy rain.
explanation.definitionFit: A pail is a vessel that holds things, and the verb describes rain falling heavily, as in bucketing down.

clue.text: Jack, always against leaving scoff

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so those letters drop out of the word

blocks.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in cards
ever means always
v is short for versus, against

explanation.surface: Jack is always objecting to people walking out of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' suggests eating greedily (British slang), but here it means mock; EVER loses V to give EER.
explanation.definitionFit: To jeer is to mock or ridicule, which is the sense of scoff as an expression of derision.

clue.text: Composer going round end of The Strand

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is kept
going round something means encircling it, so the outer word wraps the letter

blocks.note: J S Bach, the German composer
last letter of The

explanation.surface: A composer strolling around the end of the Strand, the famous London street.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a well-known street in central London, which makes it look like a place name; here a strand is a shore.
explanation.definitionFit: Strand is a literary word for the shore of a sea or lake, the sandy stretch by the water.

clue.text: Deviation from a straight – old city tax to be invested in remedy

indicators.note: money invested in something is put into it, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city
value added tax
a cure is a remedy

explanation.surface: An ancient city's tax being put into a medicine, after departing from a straight course.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur, the ancient Mesopotamian city, is the crossword's favourite 'old city'; 'a straight' is a straight line, not a strait of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Curvature is the degree to which a line or surface bends away from being perfectly flat or linear.

clue.text: Odd renovated jet, say, on estate, possibly as fun ride

indicators.note: renovating something remakes it, so its letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written
jet is a black gemstone, an example of a gem
an estate is a British station wagon, an example of a car

explanation.surface: A strangely refitted jet plane on a housing estate, offered as a fairground thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' looks like an aircraft but is the gemstone; an estate car is the British name for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodgems are small electric bumper cars at a fairground, driven for amusement by bumping each other.

clue.text: Doctor also called inside city

indicators.note: being inside something means it is enclosed within the outer letters

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
aka, also known as

explanation.surface: A doctor who has also been summoned to work within the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Also called' is the abbreviation aka, which sits inside DR.
explanation.definitionFit: Dakar is the capital of Senegal in West Africa, a large port on the Atlantic coast.

clue.text: At which Blackpool is the main team

blocks.note: the main is a poetic name for the open sea
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A football boast: Blackpool is the leading team.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackpool is a football club, so 'main team' reads as praise; Blackpool is also a famous English coastal resort in Lancashire.
explanation.definitionFit: Blackpool lies on the Lancashire coast, a classic resort by the shore of the Irish Sea.

clue.text: Suit-shortening tool

indicators.note: making something shorter trims its tail, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: one of the four card suits

explanation.surface: A tailor's gadget for taking up the length of a suit.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen makes it look like a tailoring tool; in fact the card suit loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A spade is a digging implement with a flat blade, used in gardens and on beaches.

clue.text: Etching: ‘In Bed over Sunday in Georgian Capital’

indicators.note: a capital is an initial letter, so only the first letter of the word is used

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter of Sunday, as in its short form Sun
a crib is a bed, especially a baby's
taken as written
first letter of Georgian

explanation.surface: The title of an etching, like a painting of a bed in Tbilisi on a Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted title suggests an artwork in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi; 'Capital' just takes the first letter of Georgian. 'Over' places the bed after Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: Etching is cutting lines or letters into a surface, which is exactly what carving an inscription involves.

clue.text: Shads sweat it out

indicators.note: something out of order is disarranged, so the letters must be put back differently

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone telling others to endure an ordeal until it is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweat it out' reads as an idiom for enduring; 'Shads' at the start is an unusual word, a type of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The twaite is a European species of shad, a herring-like fish that swims upriver to spawn.

clue.text: Hull put under fire

blocks.note: first meaning: an outer casing, as of a nut or boat
second meaning: to bombard with artillery

explanation.surface: The city of Hull coming under bombardment.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is an English port city, which makes it look like a place under attack; as a lower-case word it means a casing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hull is the outer husk or casing of something, and shelling means attacking with explosive artillery rounds.

clue.text: Fool around next to Gulf

indicators.note: being around something means encircling it, so the outer word wraps the inner one

blocks.note: an ass is a fool
by means beside

explanation.surface: Someone messing about beside the Gulf, the Persian Gulf region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool around' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'around' is the container signal; 'Gulf' looks like a place but means a chasm.
explanation.definitionFit: A gulf can be a deep chasm or wide gap, the same sense as a bottomless pit.

clue.text: Drive home over a month

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: to ram is to drive something home forcefully

explanation.surface: Driving back home after spending a month away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive home' reads as a commute, but means to ram a point or nail in.
explanation.definitionFit: Mar is the standard calendar abbreviation for March, the third month of the year.

clue.text: Observer upset about crack supplies again

indicators.note: upsetting something tips it upside down, which in a down entry reverses the letters
being about something means around it, so the outer letters surround the inner

blocks.note: a seer is one who sees, an observer
a crack is a joke, a quip

explanation.surface: A watcher troubled by the drug trade's renewed deliveries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' and 'supplies' suggest drugs, but a crack is a wisecrack and 'supplies' is a verb meaning provides.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-equip is to furnish with fresh gear or provisions, providing them once more.

clue.text: Propose a pill when temperature’s taken

indicators.note: something taken is removed, so that letter is lost from the word

blocks.note: a tablet is a pill
first letter of temperature, its usual symbol

explanation.surface: A nurse suggesting a pill once a patient's temperature has been measured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temperature's taken' sounds like a medical routine; it actually removes T from TABLET.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage, to table a motion is to put it forward formally for discussion.

clue.text: Love mixing with a bad lot? Just what the cruise company wants!

definitions.text: Just what the cruise company wants!

indicators.note: things mixed together are stirred up, so the combined letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, O
the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A romance with a bad crowd, followed by a quip about what a cruise operator hopes for.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful description rather than a synonym: a ship operator wants every berth filled.
explanation.definitionFit: A full complement of passengers on a vessel is what any cruise line wants for profit.

clue.text: Eastern politician wrong to eject Republican leader

indicators.note: ejecting something throws it out, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for eastern
Member of Parliament
a wrong is an error
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: An Eastern politician wrongly ousting the head of the Republican party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Republican leader' looks like a phrase, but 'leader' is the definition and R comes out of ERROR.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is the supreme ruler of an empire, so the word fits the general term for a head.

clue.text: Hat, one switched between parents

indicators.note: switching two things swaps their positions, so the pair of letters is turned round
being between two things means sitting inside them, flanked on each side

blocks.note: pa and ma are parents
an is the indefinite article, meaning one

explanation.surface: A hat passed back and forth between a mother and a father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' here is the indefinite article rather than A or I, which is why it has two letters to turn round.
explanation.definitionFit: A Panama is a lightweight straw hat, popular in summer and at the beach.

clue.text: Holiday spot needing to make new arrangements

blocks.note: first meaning: a place people go on vacation
second meaning: to sort again

explanation.surface: A holiday destination that needs to rethink its plans.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the word as re-sort, to sort once more.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort is a vacation town, and re-sorting is organising items into a fresh order.

clue.text: Confront detective at party

blocks.note: a private eye is a detective
a ball is a formal party

explanation.surface: Challenging a detective at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At' simply joins the two pieces here.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball someone is to stare at them challengingly, squaring up face to face.

clue.text: Digs secondary rock group?

blocks.note: a rock group is a band
B is second-class, as in a B grade

explanation.surface: A second-rate rock band, or one that excavates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' looks like a verb but is British slang for lodgings; a B and B is a bed-and-breakfast guesthouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Digs is informal British for rented lodgings, and a bed-and-breakfast provides a room for paying guests.

clue.text: Dance and cry loudly to audience

indicators.note: what reaches an audience is what they hear, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: to bawl is to cry loudly

explanation.surface: A performer dancing and weeping noisily before the spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words sound the same in most accents.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball is a large formal social gathering held for dancing.

clue.text: Old-fashioned stage’s position on field

blocks.note: square is slang for conventional, unfashionable
a leg is a stage of a journey; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: An outdated theatrical stage finding its place on a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' suggests a theatre but means a leg of a journey; square leg is a fielding position in cricket, level with the batsman on the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, square leg is where a fielder stands beside the batsman, at right angles to the pitch.

clue.text: A sticky sweet?

blocks.note: surface reading: a candy that is gooey and clings to the fingers
setter's reading: a sweet that comes in the form of a stick, the British seaside candy

explanation.walkthrough: Seaside rock is a hard British candy sold in long cylindrical sticks, often with the resort's name running through it; 'sticky' means stick-shaped, not gooey.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock is a hard boiled confection sold as sticks in British coastal resorts like Blackpool.

clue.text: Water etc with this added would create a scandal

definitions.text: Water etc with this added would create a scandal

blocks.clueFragment: Water etc with this added would create a scandal
blocks.note: surface reading: something added to the water supply causing an outrage, like contamination

blocks.clueFragment: Water etc with this added would create a scandal
blocks.note: setter's reading: a suffix attached to Water and other words to name political scandals, after the Nixon affair

explanation.walkthrough: The Watergate affair brought down President Nixon, and since then the suffix has been tacked onto many words to label a scandal; 'etc' covers those other cases.
explanation.definitionFit: The ending taken from Watergate is now a standard journalistic suffix meaning a political scandal or cover-up.

clue.text: Sweet old men, unkempt with tie cut off

indicators.note: unkempt means untidy and dishevelled, so the letters are left in a mess
cutting off trims the end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: the letters taken as written
a rope is something used to tie

explanation.surface: Charming, scruffy old gentlemen whose neckties have been snipped off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet old men' reads as affectionate, but 'Sweet' is the definition and 'old' is part of the anagram; ROPE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemon drop is a hard citrus-flavoured boiled candy.

clue.text: Succeed effortlessly when in bed

indicators.note: being in something means lying inside it, enclosed by the outer letters

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
as can mean when, as in 'as I arrived'

explanation.surface: Achieving things with no effort while lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In bed' sounds like lounging around, fitting the surface, but 'in' is the container signal and 'when' supplies the inner letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To coast is to move along without exertion, and figuratively to win or progress easily.
